A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAM 3 research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support comparison, including the new Object Multiplex appendix and the relocated model and annotation cards.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation, tracking, counting, adaptation and agent experiments, with extensive ablations and supplementary results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds SAM 3 Multiplex accuracy and inference-throughput results in Appendix H.

M1.justification: Appendix H introduces SAM 3 Multiplex, implementing the shared-memory direction left as future work in v1. It groups objects into buckets for joint memory encoding, attention and decoding, preserves identities through object embeddings and mux/demux operations, and randomizes training slot assignments. This substantially changes the tracker’s computation.

E1.justification: The datasets and tasks are retained. Multiplex evaluations in Tables 43–44 reuse the video PCS and VOS benchmarks already evaluated in v1 Tables 5–6. The object-count sweep varies workload within existing multi-object tracking coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix H adds direct comparisons against the original SAM 3 and includes SAM 3.1 Multiplex, with a newly trained detector, as a reference in Table 43. Comparator lineups in the existing experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 adds a throughput evaluation over 1–128 tracked objects on one H100 using optimized implementations of both models. Multiplex PCS comparisons retain the Section F.5 protocol and explicitly hold the detector fixed, separately identifying the SAM 3.1 detector variant. Existing experimental protocols are unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 30 adds a sensitivity analysis of inference throughput versus tracked-object count, identifying single-object overhead and the crossover where Multiplex becomes faster. Existing model/data ablations, robustness evaluations and agent case studies are retained.

E5.justification: The three-split mean/standard-deviation reporting in Section F.3 and human-performance estimation in Section E.4 are unchanged. Appendix H reports point estimates without introducing repeated-run counts, uncertainty intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 43–44 and Figure 30 add substantial accuracy and efficiency results without revising earlier scores. With the same detector, Multiplex raises YT-Temporal-1B cgF1 from 50.8 to 53.5 but lowers LVVIS mAP from 36.3 to 34.2. MOSEv2 VOS improves from 60.3 to 62.3. The new H100 comparison reports 11.5 versus 2.2 FPS at 128 objects, but 33.8 versus 36.4 FPS at one object.

T1.justification: Section H.1 adds a limited computational-count argument: object-specific memory passes become bucket-level passes scaling as ceil(N/M), with 3M candidate masks and 5M decoder tokens per bucket. Existing loss and metric definitions remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same principal contributions and performance claims concerning PCS, SA-Co, the SAM 3 architecture and the data engine. Multiplex is introduced in the appendix without revising those core statements.

C2.justification: Appendix H adds a mechanism explanation based on largely spatially disjoint object memories and identity-preserving embeddings. It also discusses single-object overhead and mixed benchmark accuracy. The original general limitations remain, including Section B’s future-work wording about shared memory.

D1.justification: v2 specifies Multiplex’s default 16 slots, token counts, slot randomization, H100 hardware and internal timing optimizations intended for the SAM 3.1 release. It also identifies Cityscapes evaluation as validation-set evaluation and labels Table 42’s metric as cIoU; these clarify existing experiments rather than demonstrate changed settings.

R1.justification: Appendix H positions Multiplex as an adaptation of established multiplexing and shared-identity video segmentation, adding citations to Murahari et al. (2022), Yang et al. (2021), Yang and Yang (2022), and Heo et al. (2025). The SA-FARI citation update refers to the same previously used dataset.

P1.justification: v2 inserts Appendix H and renumbers the model and annotation cards as Appendix I. Other edits are limited to annotation-card wording, metric/split clarification, a spelling correction and acknowledgements; the main narrative is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds the Multiplex architecture diagram, throughput plot and two comparison tables (Figures 29–30, Tables 43–44). Existing figures and tables undergo some relocation and pagination changes, and Table 42’s caption gains its metric label. The original visual material is retained.

improvement.justification: Appendix H develops and tests the shared-memory remedy left as future work in v1, improving the paper’s practical treatment of multi-object inference costs. Controlled accuracy comparisons and the throughput sweep make the benefits and tradeoffs assessable. The gain is focused: some accuracies regress, single-object tracking slows, and timing relies on disclosed internal optimizations; the original core claims and supporting evidence remain unchanged.
